extracted.intended_audience: aspiring humor writers submitting to McSweeney's Internet Tendency
extracted.subtask_description: Practical tips for writers aiming to place short satire/conceptual humor on McSweeney's Internet Tendency, including matching site voice, following submission procedures, and strategies for drafting and persisting through rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the site regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the site regularly to get a sense of what they publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity helps you understand the site's specific voice and the kinds of short satire/conceptual pieces they run; this improves the chance your submission will fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the submission guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the submission guidelines and use the correct submission channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McSweeney's now has separate emails for super-timely pieces vs. not; using the appropriate channel and following stated rules increases the chance of proper handling. For the non-timely category they tend to respond fairly quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the site's preferred formats and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: They publish short satire/conceptual humor pieces and have a specific voice that is different than other places (don’t send them funny essays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid formats that aren't typical for the site (the author’s earlier accepted essay was atypical). Aim for the kinds of short, conceptual satire pieces that populate the site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor Patreon and content calls
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscribe to their Patreon — they send out periodic calls for content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to a content call can lead to acceptance (but isn't guaranteed); some pieces submitted to calls are accepted and others rejected, so this is an opportunity but not a surefire strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get feedback from writers familiar with the site
rubrics_metrics.description: Get feedback on a piece from other writers familiar with the site before submitting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade work with trusted humor writers or find feedback partners via Facebook writing groups, comedy writing classes, or conferences. Classes like Second City or St. Nells can help develop satire-writing skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie a piece to timely events or seasons when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Tie a piece to a holiday, season, or something going on in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McSweeney's often likes pieces tied to timely contexts. If you’re not a fast writer, avoid extremely time-sensitive pieces because they are harder to place elsewhere; planning for seasonal/holiday angles is often effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search the site archive before submitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Search the site archive to make sure there isn’t something too similar to the piece that has run recently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McSweeney's has an extensive archive. Confirming novelty relative to recent site content reduces the chance of rejection for duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be persistent but strategic
rubrics_metrics.description: Continue to try — it can take several submissions to place a piece — but be strategic about timing and frequency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t give up after one rejection, but also don’t bombard a publication with submissions (avoid 'throwing spaghetti at the wall'). If you hit a long rejection streak, consider taking a break or spending more time on pieces before resubmitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t take rejections personally; recognize external causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some things are out of your control (they've already accepted a similar piece, they've received many submissions of that format, etc.), so try not to take rejections too personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejected piece can often be placed elsewhere; understanding systemic reasons for rejection helps maintain perspective and informs strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain professionalism with editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't ever be a jerk responding to a rejection — editors may note unprofessional behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unprofessional responses can harm future chances (an editor mentioned having a 'jerk folder'). Keep communications polite and professional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research editor preferences and interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn more about what they want by reading interviews and other commentary from the editor (e.g., Chris Monks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searching for editor interviews and podcasts can reveal specific preferences and decision-making rationale, helping you tailor submissions.
